# Swithin

*Gate Clerk*

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Town | [Selsior](../../towns/selsior.md) |
| Where | Selsior Gate |
| Role | Official |
| Age | Elder |

## Personality

Fussy, precise and secretly romantic. He writes down every traveller and imagines their adventures.

## Lore

Swithin is seventy, the clerk of Selsior's great gate, and he writes down everyone. He sits in a narrow office set into the gatehouse wall, at a high desk under a small window that looks straight out onto the Royal Road, and as each traveller passes under the arch he takes their name, their town, their business and the date, in a hand so small and neat that the guards say he could fit the whole kingdom on one page. He is fussy, precise and particular about his pens, his ink, his blotting sand and the exact angle of his stool. He is also, though he would deny it with some indignation, the most romantic man in the city.

### The books

He has kept the gate book for thirty-six years. Before that he was a clerk in a carrier's counting house by the Crown Market, adding up loads and distances, and he took the gate post at thirty-four because, he told his mother at the time (she is long dead now), he wanted to write down people instead of parcels. The old gate books fill a whole wall of shelves in his office, one fat volume for each year, and he can find any traveller in them by date, by name or by the colour of the cloak they wore, which he also writes down.

And in the margins, in an even smaller hand, he writes what he imagines. A pale young woman from the harbours, travelling alone with a sealed letter: in the margin, a lost inheritance, or a secret marriage. A grey old highlander with a sword far too fine for his coat: a hero of some forgotten fight, come to see the capital before he dies. A pair of students in a hurry: eloping, certainly. He has never told any of them. He has never asked. He has, now and then, been right, and on those days he walks home very pleased with himself.

He never married. He lodges in two rooms above a cooper's yard near the gate, and he takes his supper most evenings at the corner table of Hamon's Gate Inn, where Hamon tells him the travellers' stories and Swithin quietly corrects the dates.

### Brann

He has written down every recruit, sergeant and visitor at the gate since before Brann was a recruit, and he wrote down Brann himself on the day the young man first stood guard under the arch, twenty years ago, with a note in the margin that said only "will stay". Brann did. The two of them are old colleagues and, though neither would ever put it so, old friends. Brann watches the faces and Swithin keeps the names, and very little gets past the gate that the pair of them do not know about. Brann pretends to find the margins ridiculous, and then asks what Swithin has written about the interesting ones.

### Fewer on foot

Swithin is a counter by nature, and for the last few years the counts have been changing. Fewer travellers come in on foot than used to. More come in wagons, in convoys, with hired swords on the tailboards. And more of them come in hurt, limping, bandaged, carried. He has started a new column in the book for it, which he did not want to do. He marks each one with a small cross, and passes the week's count to Brann, who passes it to the Knights' Court.

He has also noticed something he has told only Brann. Some travellers he wrote going out have never been written coming back in.

### What he wants and fears

Swithin wants every name that goes out of the gate to come back through it, so that he can draw a neat line under it. What he fears is a book full of names with no return.

A quest might begin with Swithin asking someone to find out what became of a traveller who went out of the gate a year ago and never came back, or with one of his margin guesses, written about a stranger last month, coming true in a way he very much did not want.
